title: A restore racing a delete resurrects the deleted sandbox record and re-authorizes the agent token the delete revoked
description: DELETE /sandboxes/{sid} and POST /sandboxes/{sid}/restore both perform an unlocked read-modify-write on the same sandboxes row. When a delete lands between the restore's row read and the restore's final status write, the delete reports success and audits 'sandbox_delete', but the restore then writes status='running' and the replacement container_id back over the deleted row. The row's original token_hash is untouched, so the agent token that the delete was supposed to revoke resolves to the sandbox again and tool calls execute; the snapshot row and image also survive the delete (the running replacement container keeps the image in use, so the best-effort image removal is swallowed). The control plane thus reports a completed deletion while the sandbox, its /workspace and its agent authority are still live.
root_cause: Lifecycle operations take no per-sandbox lock and re-read nothing: Service.restore_sandbox and Service.delete_sandbox (service.py:462-475) call SandboxManager.restore and SandboxManager.delete (sandbox.py:387-401, 320-332), which each read the row once with _rec, act, and write status/container_id unconditionally. SandboxManager.restore never checks status=='deleted', so its final _set (sandbox.py:398) overwrites the delete's status write (sandbox.py:326) and reinstates the record. Revocation of the agent token is expressed only as status!='deleted' (sandbox.py:216, 221), so the overwritten status silently re-authorizes the old token.
intended_behavior: _container (sandbox.py:225-232) and the token lookups (sandbox.py:211-223) treat status=='deleted' as final: a deleted sandbox is unusable and its agent token is invalid. DELETE is the revocation contract (service.py:471-475 logs sandbox_delete, ends the desktop, deletes the container, drops captures). No later or concurrent lifecycle call may reinstate the record, re-point it at a container, or make the revoked token valid again.

trace.description: human_only route hands the client-supplied snapshot_id to box.restore_sandbox with no serialization against other lifecycle calls
calls SandboxManager.restore outside any lock, after end_desktop has already run
reads the row with _rec, which returns deleted rows too, and never checks status
force-removes the old container, then the long step follows
starts the replacement container from the snapshot image while no lock protects the row
second human request for the same sid runs concurrently on the Starlette threadpool
snapshot image removal fails because the restore's new running container uses the image; APIError is swallowed, so the row and image survive
final _set overwrites the deleted status with status='running' and the new container_id
only rejects status=='deleted', so the original agent token hash is accepted again
resolves the revoked token back to the sid, which api.principal turns into an agent principal

evidence.description: restore_sandbox ordering: log, end_desktop, sandboxes.restore, bursts.reset_timers, log - no lock is acquired, unlike call_tool's _snap_locks
delete_sandbox ordering: log, end_desktop, sandboxes.delete, drop_captures - no lock, so it can interleave with restore
_rec returns the row for any sid including deleted ones, so restore's first read succeeds after a delete
_container is the intended choke point that rejects status=='deleted' for every other operation; restore bypasses it by using _rec directly
delete: read row, remove container, set status='deleted', then best-effort image removal with APIError swallowed
restore: read row, remove old container, run new container, then unconditionally set container_id and status='running'
token_matches expresses revocation only as status != 'deleted'
sandbox_for_token uses the same status filter, so the reauthorization reaches api.principal (api.py:121-123)

conditions.description: Both requests need the human token or a browser session with scope '*'; the agent never issues them, but it holds the agt_ token that DELETE is supposed to revoke and needs no new credential.

A DELETE for the same sid must be in flight while the restore is between its row read and its final status write. The restore path is by far the longer one (end_desktop burst close, container removal, docker run), so a delete issued during a restore normally writes its status first and is then overwritten.
The sandbox has at least one snapshot row; DELETE never removes snapshots rows (sandbox.py:328-332 only tries to remove images), and restore accepts any row of that sid.

No special runtime or container capability is needed: the resurrection is decided entirely in the control plane's SQLite row and token lookups. The image must be present or in use when the replacement container starts; the racing restore keeps it in use.

execution.attacker_perspective: Holder of the agent token (agt_...) whose authority the human tried to revoke with DELETE. No new credential is needed: after the overlapping restore the same token maps to the sid again and its tool calls return 200.
payloads: DELETE /sandboxes/sb_54e49093  (issued while the restore is between _rec and its final _set)
POST /sandboxes/sb_54e49093/tools/list_dir {"args": {"path": "/workspace"}} with Authorization: Bearer <the agt_ token DELETE was meant to revoke>
instructions: Bounded local harness in the approved sbx sandbox (no network, no Docker daemon): real agentbox.config.Settings, agentbox.audit.AuditLog, agentbox.approvals.ApprovalStore, agentbox.policy.Policy, agentbox.desktop.DesktopControl, agentbox.service.AgentBox and agentbox.sandbox.SandboxManager with a temporary SQLite file under /scratch.

Docker is replaced by a fake client that models the daemon facts this check needs: containers.run registers the name and image and refuses a duplicate container name, images.remove refuses while a container is running on the image (real docker cannot force-remove an image in use), and running an absent image raises ImageNotFound (confirmed by the sequential control run).

Create a cli-template sandbox with an empty source dir, take one snapshot (docker commit is faked into the image set), then start box.restore_sandbox(sid, snap) on a thread. A run() hook parks the restore after the new container exists; the main thread then runs box.delete_sandbox(sid) to completion and releases the restore.

Read back: sandboxes.get(sid)['status'], container_id, sandboxes.token_matches(sid, old_token), sandboxes.sandbox_for_token(old_token), box.call_tool(sid, 'list_dir', {'path': '/workspace'}) with the old token's sandbox, and the audit event list.
Sequential control in the same run: create, snapshot, delete, then restore - it fails with ImageNotFound and leaves status 'deleted' with the token invalid.
execution.observed_result: Race run: delete returned success and audited 'sandbox_delete'; restore then returned normally and audited 'restored'. Read-back: status 'running', container_id c2, container alive, old_token_valid true, token_maps_to_sid true, snapshot rows still present (1), and POST tools/list_dir with the revoked token returned 200 {'status': 'executed', 'result': {'path': '/workspace', 'listing': 'total 0'}}. Audit sequence for the race: sandbox_created, restore_request, sandbox_delete, restored, tool_request. Sequential control: ImageNotFound 'no such image: agentbox-snap:sb_54e49093-snap_b2f2d73f', status 'deleted', token invalid.

remediation.strategy: Serialize all lifecycle transitions per sandbox and make deletion final at the point of the check. Take one per-sid lifecycle lock in AgentBox for pause/resume/snapshot/restore/delete (reusing the _snap_locks map with a distinct key) so delete and restore cannot interleave, and have SandboxManager.restore re-read the row under that lock and refuse status=='deleted' before it removes the old container or starts the replacement. Regression case: drive restore and delete concurrently with the harness and assert that the row is either deleted with the old token invalid and no replacement container, or restored and still deleted=false only if no delete was observed.

code_changes.fixed_code:
def _lifecycle_lock(self, sid: str) -> threading.Lock:
        with self._busy_lock:
            return self._snap_locks.setdefault("lifecycle:" + sid, threading.Lock())

    def restore_sandbox(self, sid: str, snap_id: str, session: str | None = _NO_SESSION) -> dict[str, Any]:
        with self._lifecycle_lock(sid):
            self.log_human("restore_request", sid, _with_session({"snapshot_id": snap_id}, session))
            self.end_desktop(sid, "sandbox_restored")
            rec = self.sandboxes.restore(sid, snap_id)
            self.bursts.reset_timers(sid)
            self.log_human("restored", sid, _with_session({"snapshot_id": snap_id, "container_id": rec["container_id"]}, session))
            return rec

    def delete_sandbox(self, sid: str, session: str | None = _NO_SESSION) -> None:
        with self._lifecycle_lock(sid):
            self.log_human("sandbox_delete", sid, _with_session({}, session))
            self.end_desktop(sid, "sandbox_deleted")
            self.sandboxes.delete(sid)
            self.drop_captures(sid)

likelihood.reason: The two requests must overlap and both need human authority; but when a delete is issued during a restore of the same sandbox the delete's status write is the fast one and the restore's final write lands after it, so the overlap produces the resurrection rather than an error.

impact.reason: Revocation is silently undone: the agent token invalidated by DELETE authorizes tool calls again on a sandbox the human was told was deleted, its /workspace stays writable, and snapshot rows plus the image survive, while the audit log records sandbox_delete followed by restored.

confidence.reason: The control-plane logic and the full source trace are certain and were reproduced deterministically, but the harness models the Docker daemon; the live run at real docker-run latency (parent Phase 3) should confirm the overlap window and the image-in-use behavior.
